shifts-movements-s1.title: A coffee shop's busy month
shifts-movements-s1.text: A coffee shop graphs the price of its iced latte against the number sold each day, with one downward curve labeled D for its customers' demand. Over one month: in week 1 the shop cuts the price of a latte from \$5 to \$4. In week 2 a large office building opens next door. In week 3 a rival cafe across the street starts giving away free iced tea.

items.q: Buyers' incomes rise, and at every price they now want more concert tickets than before. Shift the right curve the right way.

why.correct: More tickets wanted at every price is a shift of D to the right. Price did not cause it, so it is not a movement along D.

slips.S: Incomes belong to buyers, so they move the demand curve D; sellers' costs would move S.

items.q: A storm destroys a third of the orange groves, so at every price growers can offer fewer oranges. Shift the right curve the right way.

why.correct: Fewer oranges offered at every price is a shift of S to the left.

key.because: a storm that destroys orange groves

slips.D: The storm changes what growers can offer, so it moves S, not the buyers' curve D.

items.q: The price of concert tickets rises and nothing else changes. Place point X where buyers end up on the curve D.

why.correct: A change in price, the variable on the vertical axis, moves buyers along D: a higher price and a smaller quantity, up and to the left. The curve itself stays put.

items.q: On a graph with price on the vertical axis, which change causes a movement along a curve rather than a shift of it?
options: A change in the incomes of the good's buyers
A change in the price of the good itself
A change in the number of sellers
A change in buyers' tastes

why.correct: Only a change in a variable on one of the axes moves you along the curve; price is on the vertical axis.
options: Income is not on either axis, so it shifts the curve.
Right: price is on an axis, so it moves along the curve.
The number of sellers is not on an axis, so it shifts a curve.
Tastes are not on an axis, so they shift the curve.

items.q: A curve "shifts right". On a graph with quantity on the horizontal axis, what does that mean?
options: At every price, the quantity is larger than before
At every quantity, the price is lower than before
The price rose and the quantity rose along the same curve
The curve became steeper

why.correct: A shift right moves every point of the curve to a larger quantity at the same price.
options: Right: the same prices now go with larger quantities.
This reads the move vertically; "right" means larger quantities.
Moving along one curve is a movement, not a shift.
A change in steepness is a change in slope, not a shift right.

items.q: Why does an economist say "ceteris paribus" when drawing a curve?
options: To say the curve is a straight line
To say the two variables have a direct relationship
To say the curve will shift soon
To hold everything except the two graphed variables constant

why.correct: Ceteris paribus, "other things equal", fixes every other influence so the curve shows only how the two graphed variables relate. When one of those other things changes, the curve shifts.
options: The phrase says nothing about shape.
The phrase says nothing about the direction of the relationship.
It holds things fixed; a shift happens when one of them changes.
Right: it holds the other influences fixed.

items.q: A student reads a graph and says, "The price fell, so the curve D shifted right." What is wrong with the claim?
options: A fall in price shifts D left, not right
Price is on the horizontal axis, so it does not move D
A change in price moves along D; it does not shift D
Nothing: a lower price shifts D right

why.correct: Price is on an axis. A lower price moves buyers down along the same curve to a larger quantity.
options: Price does not shift D in either direction.
Price is on the vertical axis of a market graph.
Right: price moves you along the curve.
A lower price raises the quantity along D; the curve itself stays put.

items.q: Make the explanation specific: a cafe raises the price of its muffins and sells fewer. Fill in each blank.

why.correct: A change in the variable on an axis is a movement along the curve; anything else shifts it.

specific.frame: The ___ changed, and it is the variable on ___, so the graph shows ___.

variable.label: What changed
options: price of muffins
number of buyers
buyers' tastes

why.1: The scenario changes the muffin price; the number of buyers is not mentioned.
why.2: Nothing in the scenario changes tastes; only the price moves.

because.label: Where it sits
options: the vertical axis
neither axis

why.1: On a market graph price is on the vertical axis.

change.label: What the graph shows
options: a movement along the curve
a shift of the curve

why.1: Only a change in something off the axes shifts the curve; a price change moves along it.

specific.model: The price of muffins rose, and price is the variable on the vertical axis, so the cafe moves along its curve D to a smaller quantity because buyers want fewer muffins at a higher price.

items.q: In week 1 the coffee shop cuts the latte price from \$5 to \$4. How does its graph show this?
options: A shift of the whole curve D to the right, at each price
A movement down along D to a larger quantity
A shift of D to the left
A movement up along D to a smaller quantity

why.correct: The price is on the vertical axis, so a lower price moves down along D to more lattes sold.
options: The price change does not shift D; it moves along it.
Right: a lower price moves along D to a larger quantity.
Nothing here makes customers want fewer lattes at every price.
Up along D would be a higher price, not a lower one.

items.q: In week 2 a large office building opens next door. How does the graph show this?
options: D shifts right: more lattes are wanted at every price
A movement down along the curve D, as after a price cut
D shifts left: fewer lattes are wanted at each price
No change, because the price did not change

why.correct: More nearby customers want more lattes at every price, a change off the axes, so D shifts right.
options: Right: more buyers shift D right.
There is no price change here, so it is not a movement along D.
More customers raise the lattes wanted, not lower them.
A curve can shift even when the price stays the same.

items.q: In week 3 a rival cafe gives away free iced tea. What is the most likely change on the coffee shop's graph?
options: D shifts right: customers want more drinks
A movement up along D
A movement down along D
D shifts left: some customers drink free tea instead

why.correct: Free tea is a cheaper choice for some customers, so fewer lattes are wanted at every price: D shifts left. The latte price itself did not change.
options: Free tea pulls customers away from lattes, not toward them.
A movement along D needs a change in the latte price.
A movement along D needs a change in the latte price.
Right: fewer lattes wanted at every price.

items.q: Put the steps for deciding between a shift and a movement in order.
options: Name what changed in the scenario
Check whether it is the variable on one of the axes
If it is, move along the curve; if not, shift the curve
Show the direction with an arrow and label the new curve

why.correct: Start from the cause, test it against the axes, decide shift or movement, then show it on the graph with labels.
